newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sending officials, aid to North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sending officials, aid to North Korea.

text.p: Taipei said on Friday it would send mid-ranking officials to North Korea to monitor Taiwan's shipments of humanitarian food aid to the impoverished Stalinist state.

"We agreed last year to donate 2,000 tonnes of rice to North Korea and it should not be not surprising that we would send officials to monitor the rice shipment and delivery," a Taiwan foreign ministry official told Reuters.
Taiwan's Liberty Times quoted Foreign Minister John Chang as saying Taiwan had offered to send North Korea US$1 million in food aid and $1 million in cash.
The Liberty Times said the official delegation would be Taiwan's to North Korea, where Taipei has no diplomatic ties.
A first shipment of rice and other food left Taichung Harbour in central Taiwan on March 28 and already had arrived in North Korea, the paper said.
The foreign ministry official said Taiwan's motive in helping North Korea, a diplomatic ally of Taiwan's arch rival communist China, was not political.
The official said the donation reflected only humanitarian considerations and should not be interpreted as a Taiwan bid to promote relations with Pyongyang.
He declined to confirm media reports that several Taiwan officials would leave for Pyongyang this week.
Cash-strapped North Korea has been plagued by severe food shortages, with regular reports of imminent famine.
Local media reported that Pyongyang had acknowledged that at least 100 children had died of starvation.
Taiwan has made several moves to bolster unofficial ties with North Korea since South Korea, once its closest Asian ally, shocked Taipei by switching recognition to Beijing in 1992.
North Korea defied Chinese protests to open a Taipei travel office in 1996 and has begun doing business with Taiwan.

Pyongyang agreed in January to accept up to 200,000 barrels of low-radiation nuclear waste from state-run Taiwan Power Co for disposal in North Korea in a deal reportedly worth US$230 million -- sparking protests from South Korea.
